guide.title: Who the recipient actually sees
guide.subtitle: Automatic sender injection and when to override it
guide.excerpt: If you do not name a sender, the platform picks one from the connection that carries the message. Naming one explicitly takes priority everywhere.

sections.h: The default is to choose for you
p: A connection can have several sender numbers bound to it, each with a weight. When a request does not specify a sender, the platform injects one from the connection that ends up carrying the message, distributing across the bound numbers by weight. The caller does not have to know which number went out.
That rotation is what keeps several numbers useful: provider limits are usually per number, so spreading one connection across its numbers raises real throughput without changing anything upstream.

A sender named on the request takes priority over automatic selection. Use it when a specific number carries meaning — a support line, a national sender ID, or a number the recipient will recognize and reply to.

list: Suppression is recorded per recipient, not per sender, so switching numbers does not route around an opt-out.
A reply goes back to the number the recipient last saw, so an inconsistent sender set makes replies harder to reason about.
Automatic rotation means the sender is decided per message, not per campaign — read the message record if you need to know which one went out.
sections.scope: Sender selection and suppression are SMS-channel behavior.
